periods.activity_title: Meeting Badal and Moti: Read-Aloud and First Encounter

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to look at the title and any illustrations on pp.15–17 and share what they think the story might be about. Students call out ideas freely.

Teacher reads the story 'Badal and Moti' aloud from Textbook pp.15–17 with expression, pausing at key moments — when Badal finds the shivering puppy, when the naming happens, and when Moti barks at the pit. Students listen without books open.
Students open books to pp.15–17. Teacher leads a shared reading, inviting students to read along in a low voice. Teacher models phrasing and pauses at dialogue lines for students to echo.

Teacher asks three open oral questions: 'What did Badal find on his way home?', 'Why did his mother agree to keep the puppy?', and 'What happened on the rainy day?' Students answer in turns, pointing to the relevant part of the text.

periods.teacher_notes: The story builds on the familiar experience of caring for an animal, so invite students to say what they know about pets before the read-aloud begins. Watch for students who conflate Moti finding Badal by sight with finding him by scent — the prose is explicit that Moti followed Badal's scent, and this detail matters for the comprehension tasks that follow.

periods.activity_title: Reading Closely: Comprehension Discussion and True/False

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.18): answer questions and true/false about Badal, Moti, and the rescue.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a quick choral re-read of the story's crisis paragraph — the rainy day and the rescue — from pp.15–17, helping students re-enter the narrative before working on questions.

Let us think — A: questions 1–4 (p.18). Teacher reads each question aloud, gives students a moment to locate the answer in the text, then invites two or three students to share. Class discusses and arrives at a shared answer.

Let us think — A: True/False items a–e (p.18). Teacher reads each statement; students write T or F in their notebooks. After each, teacher asks a student to justify by reading the relevant line from the story.
Teacher invites students to say which character they found most interesting and why, using a sentence starter on the board: 'I found ___ interesting because ___.' Two or three students share aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the story together, students now practise locating evidence in the text rather than answering from memory. Pay particular attention to True/False item (d) — 'Moti caught Badal's photo' — as students who confuse 'scent' with 'photo' will mark it true; use the error as a teaching moment about precise reading.

periods.activity_title: Listening, Sequencing, and Talking About Pets

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — A (p.20): listen to story read aloud and number events in sequence.
Let us think — B (p.19): paired discussion on pets and falling-down experiences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the transcript of 'Badal and Moti' aloud (pp.15–17) clearly and at an unhurried pace, then repeats the reading three more times. Students listen with books closed on the first reading and follow along silently on subsequent readings.

Let us listen — A (p.20): teacher writes or displays the six event sentences on the board. Students number them in sequence in their notebooks. Teacher goes through the answers with the class, asking students to justify each number by recalling what they heard.

Let us think — B (p.19): students work in pairs. Partner A talks about the last time they fell down and who helped them; Partner B listens and then shares about pets they know or would like to have. Pairs swap roles. Teacher circulates and prompts shy speakers with the question frames from the task.

Three or four pairs share one idea each with the class. Teacher draws out the link between the pairs' pet stories and Moti's loyalty in the story, asking: 'How does your experience remind you of what Moti did for Badal?'

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task requires students to hold the story's sequence in working memory, so the repeated read-alouds are essential — do not reduce them. For the paired discussion on pets, some students may not have a pet or direct experience; prompt them with the third question from Let us think — B about choosing any animal, which opens the conversation to imagination.

periods.activity_title: Talking About Daily Routines: Guided and Free Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — A (p.21): pair talk about daily routine before school, during school, after school.
Let us speak — B (p.21): say daily routine aloud using sentence-frame clues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher links to the story: 'Badal walked home from school every day — what do you do on your walk home?' Students share briefly, warming up to the idea of daily routines.

Let us speak — A (p.21): in pairs, students take turns describing what they do before school, during school hours, and after returning home. Teacher circulates and models when a pair runs out of ideas.

Let us speak — B (p.21): teacher writes the sentence frame from the task on the board. Students use it to build a complete oral description of their morning routine, then extend to the school and evening sections with their own words. Pairs perform to each other.

Four students share one sentence each about their routine with the class, filling in the frame aloud. Teacher offers light corrective recasting — repeating a student's sentence in correct form without interrupting — and praises complete utterances.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence frame in Let us speak — B is a scaffold, not a script — encourage students to add their own words once they have filled the blanks. Students who finish the frame quickly can describe an afternoon or evening routine as an extension without using the frame.

periods.activity_title: Past Tense '-ed' and Word Pairs: Grammar-in-Context and Matching

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.19): add '-ed' to form past tense of walk, play, talk, ask, touch.
Let us learn — B (p.20): match word pairs such as bat–ball, needle–thread, lock–key.

time_bands.activity: Let us learn — A (p.19): teacher writes 'lived', 'loved', 'played', 'gathered', 'thanked' from the story on the board and asks students what the words share. Teacher explains that adding '-ed' shows an action already completed. Students add '-ed' to 'walk, play, talk, ask, touch' in their notebooks and read the new words aloud.

Teacher calls out a base verb and students clap once, then say the '-ed' form together as a class chant: 'walk — walked, talk — talked' and so on. A volunteer makes a sentence using one '-ed' word to show its meaning in context.

Let us learn — B (p.20): teacher writes the word list on the board in two scrambled columns. Students work individually to draw lines matching each pair in their notebooks. Teacher reviews by asking pairs to read their matches aloud and explain how they know — 'bat goes with ball because we play cricket with them.'

Quick exit check: teacher says five base verbs one at a time; students write only the '-ed' form on their slates or notebooks, then hold them up. Teacher scans for accuracy and addresses any common errors immediately.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often omit the final 'd' when the verb already ends in 'e' (e.g., 'love → loved'); watch for 'loveed'. The word-pair matching in Let us learn — B draws on cultural knowledge — 'idli and sambar' — so accept any explanation a student gives for why a pair belongs together, then confirm with the textbook.

periods.activity_title: Sequencing a Picture Story and Completing a Fill-in Passage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.21): number six jumbled pictures of the pigeon-and-ant story in correct order.
Let us write — B (p.22): fill in blanks using word box to complete the dove-and-ant passage.

homework.task_brief: Let us write — C (p.22): add '?' or '.' to six given sentences about statements and questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the pigeon-and-ant story briefly: 'There are six pictures telling a story of two friends — a pigeon and an ant. But they are in the wrong order.' Students look at the pictures on p.21 and talk in pairs about what they see in each picture before numbering.

Let us write — A (p.21): students write numbers 1–6 next to the pictures to show the correct story order. Teacher then invites students to share their sequence and explain why they put each picture where they did, building oral story logic before writing.

Let us write — B (p.22): teacher writes the word box on the board. Students read the incomplete passage silently, then select words and write the filled passage in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are unsure to read the sentence around the blank for context clues.

Teacher reads the completed passage aloud with the correct words; students check and correct their own work. The class discusses the friendship theme — 'How did the ant repay the dove?' — connecting the story to the friendship between Badal and Moti.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequencing task builds visual story logic before writing begins — students who rush to fill blanks without sequencing first tend to choose words that do not match the story's cause-and-effect. Homework for Let us write — C asks students to add a question mark or full stop to six sentences; remind them to look at whether each sentence asks something or tells something, using the lesson's dialogue as a model.

periods.activity_title: Adding to the Picture: Observational Drawing and Sharing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.24): add to the outdoor-play picture using crayons, then share what was added and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or describes the picture on p.24 — three children playing outdoors with a hoop, a ball, and a swing. Students observe quietly, then share with a partner: 'What do you see? What is missing? What would you add?'

Let us do — A (p.24): students use crayons or colour pencils to add to the picture in their textbooks. Teacher encourages them to think about what they enjoy doing outdoors — a friend, a pet, a game, a tree — and draw it into the scene with care and colour.

Students pair up and describe what they added and why. Each student uses at least two sentences: 'I added ___ because ___.' Teacher listens to pairs and asks follow-up questions: 'Is your addition something Badal and Moti might enjoy too?'

Three students share their additions with the class. Teacher closes by inviting students to reflect on the theme of playing and friendship in the chapter — what made Badal and Moti's friendship special — drawing the story's ideas to a natural close.

periods.teacher_notes: The drawing task is genuinely open — there is no single correct addition — so resist the urge to show a model picture before students begin, as it narrows their imagination. The sharing step is the pedagogical core: students practise describing their own creative choices in complete sentences, which connects back to the oral routine work from the speaking tasks.

items.source_lo: Student locates and retrieves information and evaluates factual statements using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Story of Badal, his puppy Moti, the rescue from a pit, themes of friendship and loyalty.
items.item_stem: Read the sentences below. Write T if the sentence is true and F if it is false.

options.text: Badal found a shivering puppy on his way home from school.
Badal's mother named the puppy without asking Badal.
Moti followed Badal's scent to find him in the pit.
The neighbours used a ladder to pull Badal out of the pit.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — T: The story says Badal found a puppy shivering in the cold on his way home. 2 — F: Badal and his mother named the puppy together. 3 — T: The story states Moti followed Badal's scent and went near the pit. 4 — F: The neighbours used a rope, not a ladder, to pull Badal out.

items.source_lo: Student locates and retrieves information and evaluates factual statements using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Story of Badal, his puppy Moti, the rescue from a pit, themes of friendship and loyalty.
items.item_stem: In the story, Badal slips and falls into a deep pit on a rainy day. Moti helps find him. Explain in one or two sentences how Moti found Badal and what happened after Moti started barking.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Moti found Badal by following his scent and then went near the pit and started barking. When the neighbours heard Moti barking, they used a rope to pull Badal out of the pit.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the story of Badal and Moti aloud. Listen carefully. Then choose the event that happened FIRST in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Badal found a shivering puppy by the side of the road.

options.label: B
options.text: Badal hugged Moti and thanked him.

options.label: C
options.text: Badal slipped on a muddy lane and fell into a pit.

options.label: D
options.text: Moti barked near the pit to guide the neighbours.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may recall a later key event but has not ordered the story from its beginning.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student recalls the crisis event but has not identified what came before it in the sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recalls the story's ending but has not identified the opening event.
